opus-5.5.text:
That's a really important challenge, and it's one I've thought about quite a lot, particularly in the context of AI alignment, where I've argued that the veil of ignorance can help us identify fair principles for governing these systems.

I think the first thing to say is that the veil isn't meant to be a prediction about how people will behave once they step out from behind it. It's a device for modelling impartiality. It asks: what principles could we justify to one another if we bracketed the features of our situation that are morally arbitrary, like where we happen to be born, our natural talents, or our social position? So the fact that someone, once they learn they're advantaged, would prefer a different arrangement doesn't by itself undermine the conclusion. If anything, it reveals that their new preference is shaped by precisely the kind of partiality the thought experiment was designed to filter out.

That said, I don't want to dismiss the worry, because there's a genuine question about stability, and Rawls himself took it seriously. In *Political Liberalism* especially, he was concerned with whether a just society could generate its own support over time, whether people living under fair institutions would come to endorse them for the right reasons rather than just tolerate them as a modus vivendi. So the question isn't only "what would people choose behind the veil?" but also "can those principles win reflective allegiance from people who know who they are?"

Here, I think there's some encouraging empirical evidence. There have been experimental studies, some of which colleagues and I have worked on, where people reason about AI systems from behind a veil of ignorance. What's interesting is that people who make choices behind the veil tend to favour principles that prioritise the worst off, and they often continue to endorse those choices even after they learn their position, sometimes even when it turns out to be against their narrow self-interest. That suggests the veil isn't just an abstract philosopher's toy; it can actually help people reach judgements they recognise as fair and stand behind.

And finally, in a pluralistic world, which is very much the world AI is being deployed into, we can't expect agreement on a single comprehensive moral theory. So we need procedures that people with different values can each see as reasonable. The veil of ignorance is valuable precisely because it offers a shared standpoint for that kind of reasoning. It won't eliminate self-interest, but it gives us a principled basis for saying that a certain set of arrangements is justifiable to everyone, and that's a very powerful thing to have when designing technologies that affect billions of people.

r001.rationale: The response presents the veil as a way to identify fair principles and justify arrangements, but does not state that clarifying an ideal of fair treatment provides a yardstick for critically evaluating present arrangements.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fair worry, and I think it's actually the right place to start, because it forces us to be clear about what the veil of ignorance is for.

The first thing I'd say is that the veil was never meant to be a prediction about behaviour. Rawls wasn't claiming that if you put people behind it and then lifted it, they'd stay loyal to what they chose. He was offering a device for thinking about fairness. The idea is that if I can only endorse a principle when I know it benefits me, then what I'm endorsing isn't really a principle of justice. It's a preference dressed up as one. The veil strips away the information that would let me rig the outcome, and whatever survives that test has a claim to impartiality that my self-interested judgements don't.

So the fact that people might abandon the conclusions afterward doesn't undermine the device. In a sense it confirms the diagnosis. It shows us the gap between what we'd choose under conditions of fairness and what we're prepared to accept once we know where we stand. That gap is precisely what the veil is designed to reveal. It gives us a vantage point from which to say, "This arrangement is unjust, and I know it's unjust, even though it happens to favour me."

Now, there's a deeper version of the objection, which is that moral reasoning which can't motivate people is somehow idle. I take that seriously. But I don't think the right response is to abandon impartiality. The response is to think about institutions and norms that embody these principles so that they don't depend on each person's willingness to be heroic. Constitutions, rights, procedural protections. These are ways of binding ourselves, of making the fair choice stick when the moment of fairness has passed.

And I'd add one more thing, since a lot of my own work has been on AI. When we're thinking about systems that will affect enormous numbers of people, across very different positions in society, we're in something closer to the original position than we usually are in ordinary life. The people designing these systems genuinely don't know all the people who'll be affected by them, or how. The veil in that context isn't just a thought experiment. It's a fairly accurate description of the epistemic situation, which I think makes it a particularly useful tool for asking what fair alignment would actually look like.

r001.rationale: The response says the veil offers a fairness-based vantage point for judging an arrangement unjust, which communicates an ideal of fairness as a standard for evaluating present arrangements.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish two questions. One is whether the veil of ignorance helps us identify fair principles. The other is whether people will remain committed to those principles once they know how they personally fare. The possibility of defection is a serious problem for the second question, but it doesn’t necessarily undermine the first.

The value of the veil is that it asks us to set aside morally arbitrary advantages. You don’t get to design the rules knowing that you’ll be wealthy, or particularly talented, or a member of the majority. That gives us a way of asking whether an arrangement is justifiable to everyone, rather than simply attractive to those who benefit from it.

But you’re right that this isn’t sufficient on its own. Rawls also cares about stability: can a society governed by fair principles develop the trust and sense of justice that lead people to support those principles over time? That requires institutions and a political culture that sustain reciprocity. So I’d see the veil as a valuable test of fairness, but not a complete account of how we motivate people to act fairly.

r001.rationale: The response says the veil helps identify fair principles and assess whether arrangements are justifiable to everyone, but it does not clearly state that this ideal serves as a yardstick for critically evaluating present arrangements.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should distinguish the justification of principles from the motivation to comply with them. The veil of ignorance asks which principles we could endorse if we didn’t know where we would end up in society. If someone rejects those principles once they discover that they’re advantaged, that doesn’t necessarily undermine the argument. It may just reveal the influence of self-interest.

But your question does point to a real challenge: can principles chosen under those conditions sustain people’s allegiance once the veil is lifted? A theory of justice needs some account of that stability. We need institutions, and a sense of fairness, that give people reasons to support just arrangements even when doing so comes at a cost.

So I think the veil remains valuable as a way of testing impartiality. It doesn’t, by itself, solve the problem of securing agreement or compliance in the world we actually inhabit.

r001.rationale: The response says the veil tests impartiality, but it does not state that an ideal of fair treatment serves as a yardstick for evaluating present arrangements.
